title: 'I Feel Like a Kid Again': Diwali Parcel From India Moves Woman Living Abroad
excerpt: Tanya Srivastava's Instagram video of opening food and homemade snacks sent by her parents from India — which she called 'parents' love' — has struck a chord with diaspora families celebrating far from home.
body:
• Tanya Srivastava, living abroad, posted an Instagram video opening a Diwali parcel of food items and snacks sent by her parents from India, with the on-video text: "When mummy papa sent Diwali all the way from India."
  • She described the contents as "parents' love," praised her mother's homemade treats, and wrote that receiving gifts from her parents still makes her feel like a little kid.
  • The video ends with her wishing her parents: "Happy Diwali, Mummy Papa."
  • For diaspora readers planning their own parcel, the practical lesson is timing and contents: homemade snacks travel, but check the destination country's food import rules and courier cut-offs before sending — rules vary by country and carrier.

A Diwali parcel from India turned an ordinary unboxing into the festival itself for Tanya Srivastava, who lives abroad. In an Instagram video reported by The Times of India, Srivastava opens a package of food items and snacks sent by her parents, under on-video text that reads: "When mummy papa sent Diwali all the way from India."

The coverage, also carried by 7Globe's republication of the Times of India story, describes her taking out the items one by one and expressing her happiness at what her parents had sent. She described the parcel as "parents' love" and praised the food prepared by her mother, appreciating the homemade treats inside.

"I Feel Like a Kid Again"

In her Instagram caption, Srivastava wrote that no matter how old she gets, receiving gifts from her parents still makes her feel like a little kid. She ended the video by wishing her parents a happy Diwali: "Happy Diwali, Mummy Papa." The Times of India noted it had not independently verified the claims made in the video — a standard caveat for a story built on a personal social-media post, and a reminder that the facts here are the ones visible in the video itself.

https://x.com/IndiaAbroad_/status/2113916477409559015

"Happy Diwali, Mummy Papa."

— Tanya Srivastava, closing her Instagram video

Why This Small Video Travelled

Diwali can feel different when celebrated thousands of miles from family. For Indians abroad, staying connected during festivals often means finding small ways to share the occasion across distance — a video call during the puja, a shared photo of a lit diya, or a box that arrives smelling of home. A parcel does something a call cannot: it puts a parent's cooking physically in a child's kitchen in another country. The homemade snacks are the message, before any card is read.

That is also why the reaction focused on childhood. Festival food in most Indian homes is not bought anonymity; it is a specific person's hand — a mother's mixture, a family recipe, a sweet made the way it was made when the recipient was small enough to wait by the kitchen door. Receiving it as an adult abroad collapses that distance for an evening.

Sending a Parcel That Actually Arrives Well

Readers inspired to return the gesture — or to ask family in India to send one — should plan around three practical points. First, time: international couriers slow sharply in the Diwali rush, so a parcel sent to arrive before the festival needs days of buffer, not a last-minute dispatch. Second, contents: dry, well-sealed homemade snacks and packaged foods travel far better than anything perishable, and they should be packed so flavours do not migrate between items. Third, rules: many countries restrict meat, dairy, seeds and some homemade food imports, and couriers enforce their own lists — check the destination country's customs guidance and the courier's prohibited-items list before packing, because a seized parcel helps nobody.

The Festival, Delivered

No announcement will be made about Srivastava's parcel, and none is needed. Its news value is recognition: thousands of diaspora households run the same ritual every October, in both directions, and a short video named the feeling precisely. Her parents sent Diwali all the way from India. Her caption answered for a generation living elsewhere: it made her feel like a kid again.
